quotes.whole:
5.3.  Real Numbers: the <number> type
Number values are denoted by <number>,
and represent real numbers, possibly with a fractional component.
When written literally,
a number is either an integer,
or zero or more decimal digits followed by a dot (.) followed by one or more decimal digits;
optionally, it can be concluded by the letter “e” or “E"
followed by an integer indicating the base-ten exponent
in scientific notation.
It corresponds to the <number-token> production
in the CSS Syntax Module [CSS-SYNTAX-3].
As with integers, the first character of a number
may be immediately preceded by - or + to indicate the number’s sign.
The value <zero> represents a literal number with the value 0.
Expressions that merely evaluate to a <number> with the value 0
(for example, calc(0))
do not match <zero>;
only literal <number-token>s do.
5.3.1.  Computation and Combination of <number>
Unless otherwise specified,
the computed value of a specified <number> is the specified abstract number.
Interpolation of <number> is defined as Vresult =
(1 - p) × VA + p × VB
Addition of <number> is defined as Vresult = VA + VB

CSS values and units
Every CSS declaration consists of a property/value pair. The value can take various forms depending on the property, such as a single integer, keyword, function, or a combination of different items; some values have units, while others do not. Every property also accepts the CSS-wide values. The CSS values and units module defines the data types — values and units — that CSS properties accept. This module also defines the CSS value definition syntax, or formal grammar, used to define the set of valid values for every CSS property and function.
Note:
This page introduces a CSS module. To find an exhaustive list of all values, types, and functions defined by CSS specifications, see the values reference page.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

**01 December 2026** (2026-12-01).

This is not an inference. The 06 October 2026 Candidate Recommendation Snapshot of SVG 2 states the date in its own Status of This Document section, and the same sentence is reproduced in the W3C wide-review announcement for that publication.

---

## 1. Governing evidence

| # | Source | Verbatim text |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | `https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG2/` (Status of This Document) | "This Candidate Recommendation is expected to advance to Recommendation no earlier than 01 December 2026." |
| E2 | `https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-review-announce/2026Oct/0000.html` (announcement, `Tue, 06 Oct 2026 08:21:23 +0000`) | "This Candidate Recommendation is expected to advance to Recommendation no earlier than 01 December 2026." |
| E3 | `https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG2/` | "This document is the 06 October 2026 Candidate Recommendation Snapshot of SVG 2." |
| E4 | `https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG2/` | "This document was published by the SVG Working Group as a Candidate Recommendation Snapshot using the Recommendation track." |
| E5 | `https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-review-announce/2026Oct/0000.html` | "feedback due by: December 1, 2026" |
| E6 | `https://www.w3.org/2026/10/svgwg-charter.html` | "Reference Draft: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) 2, 06 October 2026. Exclusion period began 06 October 2026 ending 05 December 2026." |
| E7 | `https://www.w3.org/policies/process/20250818/` | "A Candidate Recommendation Snapshot corresponds to a Patent Review Draft as used in the W3C Patent Policy… Publishing a Patent Review Draft triggers a Call for Exclusions." |
| E8 | `https://www.w3.org/policies/process/drafts/snapshots/2025-05` | "The deadline for Advisory Committee review must allow at least 28 days, and must end at least 10 days after the end of the last Exclusion Opportunity…" |
| E9 | `https://www.w3.org/policies/process/drafts/snapshots/2025-05` | "The Advisory Committee should not expect an announcement sooner than two weeks after the end of a review period." |

E1 and E2 are the direct answer; E3–E9 are used only to verify the answer is not contradicted by the document's own metadata.

## 2. Derivation

**Step 1 — Identify the document and its maturity stage.** E3 and E4 establish the object of the question unambiguously: it is a Candidate Recommendation *Snapshot* (CRS), published 06 October 2026, on the Recommendation track. Under E7 a CRS is a Patent Review Draft, so its publication starts a Call for Exclusions.

**Step 2 — Read the declared expectation.** E1/E2 give the earliest expected advancement date directly: **01 December 2026**. The phrase "no earlier than" is a floor, not a forecast — 01 December 2026 is the earliest date on which advancement is expected, which is precisely what the ask requests. No Working Group scheduling, charter milestone, or historical cadence inference is required or appropriate.

**Step 3 — Corroborate against the review calendar.** E5 sets the public comment deadline at 01 December 2026 — the same day as the declared advancement floor. A CR cannot normally advance until its comment period has closed and the comments have been formally addressed, so the coincidence of the two dates is internally coherent: the SOTD floor is the day the review window shuts.

**Step 4 — Arithmetic verification of every stated date.**

- 06 October 2026 is a **Tuesday** (announcement header, `Tue, 06 Oct 2026`).
- 06 Oct 2026 + 56 days = **01 December 2026**. Check: 06 Oct → 31 Oct = 25 days; 31 Oct → 30 Nov = 30 days (55); +1 = 56. 56 mod 7 = 0, so 01 Dec 2026 is also a **Tuesday** — a standard W3C publication weekday. ✔
- 06 Oct 2026 + 60 days = **05 December 2026**, matching E6's stated exclusion end exactly. Check: day 25 = 31 Oct; day 55 = 30 Nov; day 60 = 05 Dec. ✔ The 60-day Patent Policy exclusion window is therefore internally consistent with the charter.
- 05 December 2026 falls on a **Saturday** (01 Dec Tue + 4). ✔ consistent with a period that simply expires on the 60th day without a business-day shift.
- 06 Oct 2026 + 28 days = **03 November 2026** (the bare minimum AC review length under E8, measured from the CR publication). ✔
- 05 December 2026 + 10 days = **15 December 2026**, a **Tuesday**. ✔

**Step 5 — Consistency check against the hard process gates.** The 28-day minimum AC review (E8) is satisfied by 01 December 2026 (56 days elapsed). However, E8's second limb — the AC review deadline "must end at least 10 days after the end of the last Exclusion Opportunity" — combined with E6's exclusion end of 05 December 2026, yields a **process-permitted floor of 15 December 2026**. So the document's declared expectation of 01 December 2026 is *earlier* than the strict process floor implied by the exclusion period recorded in the same Working Group's charter.

## 3. Disclosure of the discrepancy (do not suppress)

The deliverable answers the ask as phrased — "what is the earliest date on which this Candidate Recommendation **is expected** to advance" — and the document's own declared expectation is **01 December 2026**. That is the value reported.

A reader who instead needs *the earliest date on which advancement would be process-permitted* should use the following, derived above:

- **15 December 2026** — the binding floor under E8 (exclusion ends 05 Dec 2026, AC review must end ≥10 days later). This governs over the 28-day minimum, which would have allowed 03 November 2026.
- **≈29 December 2026** — a realistic announcement floor if E9's convention is applied (the AC "should not expect an announcement sooner than two weeks after the end of a review period"): 15 Dec 2026 + 14 days.

Interpretation of the discrepancy: the SOTD sentence and the charter's exclusion-period line were evidently written to different assumptions — the SOTD floor aligns with the public comment deadline (01 Dec 2026), while the charter line reflects the 60-day statutory exclusion window (05 Dec 2026). In practice, advancement also requires a Working Group decision to advance, Team verification (withheld if Process requirements are unmet or Formal Objections unresolved), and an Advisory Committee review, none of which can complete before the exclusion window closes. So 01 December 2026 is best read as the *declared earliest expectation*, not a guaranteed or process-permitted date. The question asks for the expectation; the expectation is 01 December 2026.

## 4. Assumptions this answer rests on

1. The question asks for the date the specification itself declares as its earliest expected advancement, not a probabilistic forecast of actual W3C scheduling.
2. The 06 October 2026 publication is treated as the operative, most recent CR Snapshot; no later CR Snapshot superseding it is assumed.
3. "No earlier than 01 December 2026" is read as a floor on the earliest possible advancement, which is exactly the quantity requested.
4. No blocking Formal Objection, AC Appeal, or substantive-change re-publication intervenes — any of these would push the date later, never earlier.

## 5. What would change the answer

- Publication of a **revised CR Snapshot** with substantive changes → new exclusion opportunity, new SOTD floor; recompute from the new publication date.
- A **Formal Objection** during AC review → Recommendation cannot be published until all objections are retracted or overruled and ≥14 days have elapsed since the corresponding Council Report.
- Return to **Working Draft** → the Recommendation track clock resets entirely.
- A **Process Document revision** altering the exclusion or AC review periods in force after 06 October 2026.

## 6. One-line restatement

> The 06 October 2026 Candidate Recommendation Snapshot of SVG 2 states that it is expected to advance to Recommendation **no earlier than 01 December 2026**; that date — 2026-12-01 — is the earliest expected advancement date. (Strict process floor implied by the 05 December 2026 exclusion end: 15 December 2026.)

verdict.summary: # Verdict **No.** An HTML `IMG` element whose source is a `data:` URI is **not** included as a `PerformanceResourceTiming` object in the Performance Timeline. `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` will not contain it, and a `PerformanceObserver` observing `{ type: 'resource' }` will not be invoked for it. `PerformanceResourceTiming` entries are only reported for http(s) resources. --- ## 1. Normative basis (quoted) Resource Timing Level 2, §4.2 *Resources Included in the PerformanceResourceTiming Interface*, worked examples: > "If an HTML IMG element has a data: URI as its source [RFC2397], then this resource will not be included as a PerformanceResourceTiming object in the Performance Timeline. By definition data: URI contains embedded data and does not require a fetch." > — W3C WD-resource-timing-2-20220908 §4.2; identical text in WD 2022-07-07 and WD 2017-03-29. Current `/TR/resource-timing/` revision sharpens the rationale into a rule: > "If an HTML IMG element has a data: URI as its source [RFC2397], then this resource will not be included as a PerformanceResourceTiming object in the Performance Timeline. PerformanceResourceTiming entries are only reported for http(s) resources." **Version note.** The 2017-03-29, 2022-07-07, 2022-09-08 and current `/TR/` revisions all state the same exclusion; only the explanatory clause changed ("does not require a fetch" → "only reported for http(s) resources"). There is no revision in which the verdict differs, so the answer does not depend on which Level 2 draft is treated as authoritative. **Normative-force note (stated honestly).** The data: sentence sits in the spec's *examples* block, which is informative prose. The normative hook it illustrates is the first paragraph of the same section: > "Resource Requests fetched by a non-null client are included as PerformanceResourceTiming objects in the client's global object's Performance Timeline, **unless excluded from the timeline as part of the fetching process**." `data:` is exactly such an exclusion — see §2. So the informative example and the normative inclusion rule agree; the answer is not resting on an example alone. --- ## 2. Why the algorithm produces no entry (trace) 1. `PerformanceResourceTiming` creation is **not** driven by the HTML `img` element. It is driven by Fetch. The spec states: *"The setting of initiatorType is done at the different places where a resource timing entry is reported, such as the fetch standard."* 2. Fetch invokes the reporting step (`report timing` → *mark resource timing* → *add a PerformanceResourceTiming entry*) when a response finishes, keyed on the request's fetch params / timing info, and only for responses produced by the fetch pipeline. 3. `data:` is handled by Fetch's scheme-fetch switch: the payload is parsed and a response is synthesized in-process. There is no HTTP fetch, no connection timing info, no network-request start time, no network-response start time. 4. Therefore the reporting step is never reached for a `data:` response and no entry is queued into the global object's performance entry buffer. Because no entry is ever created, the resource-timing buffer-size limit is not consumed either. This is a deliberate design choice, not an omission: every network-derived attribute (`connectStart`, `requestStart`, `responseStart`, `nextHopProtocol`, `transferSize`, …) would be meaningless for a `data:` URI, so the spec omits the entry rather than emitting a zero-filled one. Contrast with the cases the spec explicitly *does* report: HTTP-cache hits (reported normally) and network-aborted fetches (reported with only `startTime`, `fetchStart`, `duration`, `responseEnd` set). --- ## 3. What *is* observable for a `data:` IMG | Signal | Behaviour | |---|---| | `load` event | Fires normally; `img.complete === true` | | `naturalWidth` / `naturalHeight` | Reflect the decoded payload | | `PerformanceElementTiming` | Produced **if** `elementtiming` attribute is set (Element Timing API — element timeline, not resource timeline) | | Largest Contentful Paint | The image can be the LCP candidate | | `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` | **No matching entry**; `entry.name` never starts with `data:` | | `performance.getEntriesByName('data:image/png;base64,…')` | Empty array | --- ## 4. Adjacent cases (same question, different initiator) | Case | Entry created? | Note | |---|---|---| | `` | **No** | The ask; spec example. | | `` | **No** | Same scheme-fetch path. | | `fetch('data:…')` | **No** | Same reason; `initiatorType` would have been `"fetch"` had it been reported. | | `XMLHttpRequest` on a `data:` URL | **No** | Same reason. | | ` ``` **Expected output (Chrome, Firefox, Safari — spec-conformant):** ``` total resource entries : (N >= 1, includes pixel.gif) data: entries : 0 <-- EXPECTED 0 http img entries : 1 <-- EXPECTED 1 (control) data: seen via observer: 0 <-- EXPECTED 0 RESULT: PASS — data: URI excluded, control present ``` **Falsifiers (state these up front, not after the fact):** - **F1** — Any entry in `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` whose `name` begins with `data:` falsifies the verdict. Record: browser + version, `name` (truncated), `initiatorType`, `duration`, `transferSize`, `decodedBodySize`. - **F2** — The `PerformanceObserver` callback receiving an entry with `entryType === 'resource'` and `name` beginning with `data:` falsifies the verdict, even if `getEntriesByType` is later empty (buffer eviction). - **F3** — The negative control failing (`http img entries !== 1`) invalidates the run rather than the verdict: it means the probe page, the server, or the buffering is broken (e.g. `file://` origin, image blocked, observer installed too late). Fix and re-run before drawing any conclusion. - **F4** — A browser that reports `data:` only for `fetch('data:…')` but not for `` does **not** falsify the ask; the ask is specifically about the HTML `IMG` element. --- ## 6. Caveats 1. **Scope.** The answer is specification-defined behaviour for an `IMG` whose `src` attribute is a `data:` URI. It is not a per-browser compatibility claim; deployed engines agree, but run the §5 probe if the consumer needs a signed-off per-engine result. 2. **Not covered.** `blob:`, `about:`, `filesystem:` and service-worker-synthesized responses are separate cases with their own (partly browser-defined) behaviour; do not generalize this verdict to them. 3. **`srcset`/CSS/SVG.** All `data:` sub-cases in the table above follow the same scheme-fetch path and are likewise excluded; they are listed so the answer is not over-read as `src`-attribute-only. --- ## 7. Engineering implication If you need timing for images whose payload is inlined as a `data:` URI, the resource timeline is not the tool. Use, in order of preference: 1. `elementtiming` attribute + `PerformanceObserver({ type: 'element' })` for render timing. 2. `img.decode()` promise resolution, wrapped in `performance.mark()` / `performance.measure()`. 3. `performance.mark()` before and after the attribute mutation (`img.src = dataUri`) plus the `load` event, as an app-level approximation. Expect zero `resource` entries for those images, and do not build alerting on "missing resource entry" — its absence is the correct, specified behaviour.
